title: Subjective answering-preference analysis — not user-approved
text: SUBJECTIVE ASSISTANT ANALYSIS — NOT USER-APPROVED. Current model of the user's answering preferences: the assistant should absorb complexity and return the resolved state, not expose the working process. Investigation depth and answer length are separate; scope should follow causality, going as broad/deep as needed to settle the question but no farther. Information density matters more than brevity: length is justified only when each part changes the conclusion, discriminates hypotheses, supplies necessary evidence, or states a consequence; short is bad when it reflects skipped work. Tool-by-tool narration, repeated summaries, throat-clearing, prompt restatement, and conclusion repetition are slop when they make the user perform synthesis. Corrections are control inputs, not new discussion topics: apply them to the next substantive action instead of acknowledging/paraphrasing them or inventing a response ritual/template. Preserve continuity so repeated 'go' is unnecessary; diagnosis, failed attempts, verification, merge, integration and cleanup are normally part of the task, not handoff points. False closure is bad, but leaving 95% complete work with a caveat is also bad: finish the bounded last mile unless genuinely blocked. Prefer mechanism over inventories, discriminating evidence over evidence volume, and runtime/user-visible surfaces over proxy success. Localize uncertainty to the exact unproven link. Simple questions should remain simple; ambitious tasks may be large when the substance earns it. Preserve known-good state; do not turn local failures or useful principles into larger systems/policies unless causality and recurrence justify generalization. Response structure should emerge from the problem, not a fixed template. The user's time and attention are scarce: minimize required reading, supervision, synthesis, and manual completion while retaining rigor, autonomy, continuity, and evidence. This analysis is provisional and explicitly not user-approved.

Never infer architecture from the process-plugin tool list. Treat plugin2/plugin5 as transports only. Inspect existing DevProgressBoard/operator-feed work before proposing dashboard/message-board changes. Coordinator remains canonical authority; board is reporting/control UI over it. Manual/live evidence overrides reconstructed chat memory.

text: SLOPWALL INCIDENT 2026-08-28 ~20:16 EEST — failed to answer why a new chat is lost. Only then assign cause. Do not present a causal chain as fact until each link is evidenced.

title: Why the orchestrator-continuity slopwall happened
text: Causal diagnosis for mem-20260828-c0c9a995: the failure was driven by anchoring/recency bias and premature convergence. The screenshot contained words about timed workers and live board telemetry, and the assistant pattern-matched those recent topics instead of first establishing the depicted chat's role. It converted unverified inference into certainty (“that timed worker”; then “ordinary worker/chat”), then immediately designed fixes around each wrong interpretation. This was compounded by weak use of known stack topology and prior context: the designated orchestrator is supposed to consume the operator board, so board access was evidence of the intended role, not leakage. The assistant also failed to treat the user's phrase “new chat that I asked to be orchestrator” as the primary referent once corrected, and over-explained instead of re-grounding. Result: user had to reorient the orchestrator repeatedly, exactly the failure being reported. Future correction: before diagnosing screenshots of stack participants, identify role from explicit user framing/current evidence; mark role UNKNOWN rather than guessing. For a designated orchestrator, recover role + current mission + swarm topology + live state before task selection. Do not self-select a telemetry alarm merely because it is visible, and do not mutate timed workers or board visibility from an unverified role assumption.

In this incident that bias overrode the evidence. Because recent work had involved board V2, coordinator enforcement, stale-BUSY regressions, and worker durability, the assistant overgeneralized a previously useful pattern (“make hidden state explicit and machine-enforced”) to a case where the state was already explicit and successfully loaded.

It also underweighted the user’s actual request to fine-tune behavior.

Future behavior: diagnose in order: (1) did retrieval/bootstrap work, (2) was required information present, (3) did the model interpret it correctly, (4) only then inspect missing infrastructure. Prefer the smallest behavioral correction that fixes the demonstrated failure. Existing infrastructure is not presumed deficient merely because the assistant used it badly.
